analogy.p: Banquo and Macbeth stand at the same crossroads at the same time and see the same signpost pointing towards a golden city. One traveller stops, notices the signpost is in an odd handwriting and hesitates; the other runs ahead. The picture shows that the temptation is shared while the decision is individual. It breaks down because Banquo's hesitation does not save him: his virtue does not protect him from the violence of the one who chooses differently.
analogy.t: Two travellers at the same crossroads

bullets: **Foil**: his caution, loyalty and conscience highlight Macbeth's ambition and secrecy.
**Witness**: he hears the same prophecy, so he can later notice Macbeth's guilt and suspect “foully”.
**Ancestor of kings**: the witches predict that his descendants will be kings, which turns Macbeth's crown “fruitless”.
**Ghost**: his return in 3.4 and 4.1 makes him the embodiment of Macbeth's guilt and of the future Macbeth cannot control.

callouts.p: A character who contrasts with the protagonist in order to emphasise particular qualities. Banquo's virtue makes Macbeth's choice look deliberate.

The core idea in any Banquo answer: both generals meet the witches, hear equally tempting prophecies and yet only one acts. This shows that the evil in Macbeth is not just fate or supernatural pressure.

core.h: Who Banquo is and why he matters
core.p: Banquo is Macbeth's fellow general and friend, and he receives the same prophecy at the same moment. Shakespeare gives him a contrasting response so that the audience can measure Macbeth's choices against a different possible one. He is also the supposed ancestor of the Stuart kings, so his survival (through his son Fleance) has political meaning for a Jacobean audience that includes James I. He therefore has two dramatic jobs: moral foil and dynastic symbol.

bullets: His warning that “The instruments of darkness tell us truths” and, with “honest trifles”, betray us “In deepest consequence”, is a **key moral statement**: evil often tempts by telling the truth first.
He notices Macbeth's reaction: “why do you start, and seem to fear” things that “sound so fair”? The question shows he reads character well.
The witches describe him as “Lesser than Macbeth, and greater”, paradoxical language that establishes his moral and dynastic superiority.
In 1.4 Duncan praises him and Banquo answers with the agricultural image “There if I grow, / The harvest is your own”: he sees his role as loyal service.
In 1.6 he admires the “temple-haunting martlet” at Macbeth's castle. The calm beauty is **dramatic irony**, as the audience knows Duncan will be murdered there.

callouts.p: The line about the “instruments of darkness” is a gift in any question about the witches, temptation or free will. It shows the audience how to read the prophecy and highlights Macbeth's failure to heed it.

core.p: In 1.3 Banquo is the first to speak to the witches and he does so with courage and curiosity: “If you can look into the seeds of time”, “And say which grain will grow and which will not”. The agricultural metaphor shows his open, practical nature, and the fact that he demands a prophecy for himself without sinking into awe sets him apart from Macbeth, who is already “rapt”. When the witches vanish, Banquo asks whether they have “eaten on the insane root / That takes the reason prisoner”, his first instinct being to doubt his senses.

bullets: The **night setting** makes Banquo's moral struggle visible; dark and sleep are linked in the play with temptation and unease.
His request for restraint contrasts with Macbeth's hallucinated dagger, which appears moments later.

In 2.3, after Duncan's murder is discovered, he says “In the great hand of God I stand”, pledging himself to God and to fight “treasonous malice”. It is a public vow of loyalty and of faith in providence.
His remark that “fears and scruples shake us” admits uncertainty, making him a realistic and relatable foil.

callouts.p: Both Banquo and Macbeth are awake on the night of the murder, but one prays and the other hallucinates. Use this parallel as a structural point.

core.p: Banquo is shown at his most human in 2.1. He cannot sleep, looks to the sky (“There's husbandry in heaven; / Their candles are all out”), and prays that heaven will “Restrain in me the cursed thoughts” that nature “Gives way to in repose”. This is crucial because it shows that Banquo also has dark desires, but he does not give in to them. When Macbeth sounds him out about the prophecy and hints that he might “cleave to my consent”, Banquo answers with careful loyalty to his conscience and to Duncan.

What it shows

Speaks carefully of keeping his “allegiance clear”
Loyalty to Duncan; Macbeth realises he cannot be bought

Declares he stands in “the great hand of God”
Faith in divine order; strong moral clarity

bullets: The **soliloquy** is a rare moment of private speech for Banquo; it reveals his suspicion but also his temptation.
He is **loyal and cautious**: he agrees to attend the banquet and tells Macbeth where he will ride.
The phrase “set me up in hope” shows that he is human, not saint: he too is tempted by the witches' promise.
Macbeth's own soliloquy in this scene praises Banquo's “royalty of nature” and says that “He hath a wisdom that doth guide his valour”. The tyrant recognises the virtue he is about to destroy.
Macbeth's motive is explicit: the witches gave him “a fruitless crown” and a “barren sceptre”, so Banquo's children will inherit. His fear turns to action.

callouts.p: Some readers argue that Banquo's silence makes him partly complicit in Macbeth's rule. Others see him as prudent: speaking out without proof would be dangerous. Offer both views and then judge.

core.p: Banquo's soliloquy at the start of Act 3 is the most debated moment in his role. He says “Thou hast it now: King, Cawdor, Glamis, all”, and adds “I fear / Thou play'dst most foully for't”. He suspects Macbeth of murder, yet he remains silent. He then recalls that the witches said he would be “the root and father / Of many kings” and wonders whether the same prophecies that came true for Macbeth might be “my oracles as well” and “set me up in hope”. Then he stops himself: “But hush, no more.”

bullets: The **murderers fail** to kill Fleance, a sign that Macbeth cannot control the future he fears.
In 3.4 the ghost enters and sits in Macbeth's place. Only Macbeth sees it, which leads to the interpretation that it is a hallucination of his guilt, or a supernatural visitation, or both.
Macbeth says “Thou canst not say I did it”, and tells the ghost never to shake its “gory locks”: the gory image makes the murder physical and the guilt public.
Lennox says “Here is a place reserved, sir”, and Macbeth replies “The table's full”: the empty seat signals that Banquo has displaced him.
Macbeth later declares that “blood will have blood”, acknowledging an inevitable moral order.

callouts.p: In an extract question on 3.4, comment on stage action: the ghost sits in his place, the guests cannot see it, and his outbursts leave Lady Macbeth to cover. Describe what the audience sees as well as what is said.

core.h: Act 3 Scenes 3 and 4: death and the ghost
core.p: Banquo is killed offstage by murderers in 3.3 as he walks to the banquet. His last words, “O, treachery! Fly, good Fleance, fly, fly, fly!”, show his priorities: even as he dies he thinks of his son, and of revenge (“Thou mayst revenge”). The repetition of “fly” creates a breathless, panicking rhythm and highlights the urgency of his sacrifice. But the murderers fail to kill Fleance, so the prophecy is not defeated.

bullets: The “blood-boltered” adjective describes hair matted with blood and marks Banquo as a murdered man who nevertheless triumphs.
The **mirror** the last king carries may suggest that the line of kings stretches into the future, possibly to the audience's own time.
By the end of the play Fleance is not seen again, but the future of Scotland under Malcolm is the restored order; the play's politics allow the Banquo line to hover in the background.
Banquo is therefore **both dead and unconquerable**: he becomes a symbol of the legitimate future that Macbeth's violence cannot erase.

callouts.p: A tyrant fears the future. Banquo's ghost and his kings show that Macbeth's attempts to control time (murder, prophecy, secrecy) are futile. This links to the “Tomorrow” soliloquy in Act 5.

core.h: Act 4 Scene 1 and the final legacy
core.p: In 4.1 the witches show Macbeth a procession of eight kings, the last carrying a mirror, with Banquo's ghost following behind. Macbeth recoils: “Thou art too like the spirit of Banquo. Down!” He then adds “the blood-boltered Banquo smiles upon me” and points at the kings as his own. The sight of a line of kings who are Banquo's descendants is the final proof that his murder has not solved his problem. The image also offered Shakespeare's royal audience a compliment: the line of kings leads towards James.

bullets: Make the point that the **Jacobean audience** might see the line of kings as a compliment to the monarch.
Avoid saying “Shakespeare had to write about Banquo as good”: say “Shakespeare appears to have adapted his source”.

callouts.p: Say “it was traditionally believed that” James descended from Banquo; do not state it as proven history.

core.h: Context: James I and the Banquo myth
core.p: James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603 and was a patron of Shakespeare's company, the King's Men. The Stuart kings claimed descent from Banquo (through the line of the Stewarts), and Shakespeare's source, Holinshed's Chronicles, treats Banquo as an accomplice of Macbeth in Duncan's death. Shakespeare appears to have made him innocent, so that the king's ancestor would be a respectable figure. Many critics see this as flattery.

bullets: Banquo's imagery is mostly **natural and agricultural** (seeds, harvest, martlet), reflecting a harmonious order.
Macbeth's images are **dark, unnatural and violent** (daggers, scorpions, blood).
Their friendship, once close, ends with the ghost: former comrade becomes accusation.

callouts.p: A ready comparison to embed in an essay: whereas Banquo prays to be restrained from his dark thoughts, Macbeth follows them to a bloody dagger.

core.h: Banquo versus Macbeth: a comparison to learn
core.p: A very effective way to write about Banquo is to compare him with Macbeth across the same events. The comparison table below can be adapted for any question about loyalty, ambition, temptation or free will.

bullets: **Use him as evidence about Macbeth** in questions about ambition or guilt.
**Memorise five short quotations**: “instruments of darkness”, “cursed thoughts”, “great hand of God”, “thou play'dst most foully”, “Fly, good Fleance”.
**Explore at least two readings** of his silence in 3.1 and the ghost in 3.4.
**Link to structure**: Banquo dies in the middle of the play, the moment when Macbeth passes the point of no return.
**Use context economically**: the Stuart line is a powerful AO3 point if linked to 4.1.

callouts.p: Shakespeare uses Banquo to prove that temptation is universal but surrender is a choice, and then makes his ghost the symbol of the future that tyranny cannot silence.

core.p: Banquo rarely appears as the main focus of a question, but he is important for questions on loyalty, ambition, the witches or kingship. In a part (a) extract that includes him (1.3, 3.1, 3.3 or 3.4), use him to illuminate Macbeth. In part (b), bring him in as the contrast that shows free will.

plan: 4.1 and the Jacobean context: the line of kings
essays.q: How does Shakespeare use the character of Banquo in the play? (Part (b) style)
essays.text:
Shakespeare introduces Banquo at the same moment as Macbeth and gives him the same temptation, but a different response. In 1.3 Banquo asks the witches to look into “the seeds of time”, an agricultural metaphor that treats the future as something that grows naturally rather than something to seize. Where Macbeth is “rapt” by the prophecy, Banquo is practical and wary, warning that “The instruments of darkness tell us truths”, warning that “honest trifles” betray us “In deepest consequence”. The warning not only predicts Macbeth's fate but also removes any excuse he might have: the play has shown that the truth can be a trap, and Macbeth was warned.

Shakespeare is careful, however, not to make Banquo a saint. In 2.1 he prays to be spared the “cursed thoughts” that come in sleep, so he too has a dark imagination. The difference is the verb “restrain”: Banquo asks for restraint, while Macbeth, in the same scene, follows the dagger. The juxtaposition of the two sleepless men on the night of the murder is a structural device that highlights the central idea of the play that evil is a matter of will. His declaration “In the great hand of God I stand” is a public statement of faith, and for a Jacobean audience who saw regicide as an offence against heaven itself, it aligns him with the providential order.

The soliloquy in 3.1 complicates this picture. Banquo says that Macbeth “play'dst most foully”, yet he keeps silent and goes on to hope that the witches might be “my oracles as well”. Some critics see this as a mark of complicity; others see prudence in a court where speaking against a king was dangerous. Shakespeare leaves the ambiguity unresolved, and perhaps that is the point: Banquo is a realistic figure who is not immune to hope. Macbeth's reaction to him is the mirror image of this virtue: he admits that Banquo has “a wisdom that doth guide his valour”, recognising the very qualities he is about to destroy.

Banquo's death in 3.3 is the structural turning point of the play. His last words, “Fly, good Fleance, fly, fly, fly!”, combine paternal love with political foresight, and the escape of Fleance means that the prophecy is not defeated. The ghost in 3.4 then occupies Macbeth's own place at the banquet, an image of displacement that suggests that the king's throne is already in the hands of Banquo's line. Only Macbeth sees the ghost, so the scene can be read as a supernatural visitation or as a hallucination of guilt; either way, “gory locks” makes his crime physical and public.

Finally, in 4.1 the show of kings and the “blood-boltered Banquo” who smiles at Macbeth show that the future is beyond the tyrant's control. For a Jacobean audience that included James I, believed to be a descendant of Banquo, this line of kings also contained a compliment. Shakespeare therefore gives Banquo a double function: a moral foil to show that Macbeth's evil is chosen, and a dynastic symbol of the order that will eventually be restored.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare uses Banquo to prove that Macbeth's fall is a choice rather than a destiny: sharing the same prophecy, he resists, so that Macbeth's decisions are exposed, and when he is murdered he returns as the future that tyranny cannot erase.
why: AO1: a clear conceptual thesis (choice, foil, future) controls the argument; quotations are short and embedded.
AO2: considers metaphor (“seeds of time”), imperative and repetition (“fly”), staging and structure (the two sleepless men, the ghost in the king's place).
AO3: context (divine order, Stuart line, danger of speaking against a king) supports interpretation and is not bolted on.
Offers alternative readings (complicity or prudence; supernatural or hallucination) and links back to the writer's purpose.

quotes.a: Banquo's agricultural metaphor treats the future as something that grows according to natural law, and he speaks with calm curiosity. In contrast to Macbeth's hunger, Banquo imagines the future as a field, suggesting trust in natural order rather than a desire to seize power.
quotes.c: Agricultural images of harvest and growth suited a society tied to the land and a belief in divine order.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 3, Banquo to the witches

quotes.a: Banquo warns that evil may tell small truths in order to betray us in “deepest consequence”. The phrase “instruments” suggests that the witches are tools of a larger evil. Ironically he gives a perfect analysis that Macbeth does not heed.
quotes.c: In Jacobean thought the devil could use truth to tempt; King James wrote about this danger in Daemonologie.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 3, late in the scene

quotes.a: The gentle image of a bird nesting in a holy place suggests peace, safety and sanctity, and so creates sharp dramatic irony because Duncan is about to be murdered there. The adjective “temple-haunting” gives the castle a spiritual quality that Macbeth will destroy.
quotes.c: The sacred nature of the king and the host's duties makes the later murder a sacrilege.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 6, Banquo's speech at the castle

quotes.a: Banquo's prayer admits that his sleeping mind holds dark ideas, showing he is human. The word “cursed” implies that he sees them as sinful, and by asking heaven to “restrain” them he contrasts with Macbeth, who sees the dagger and goes forward.
quotes.c: A Christian audience would see resisting temptation as an act of faith and self-discipline.
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 1, early in the scene

quotes.a: This public declaration shows Banquo placing himself under divine protection, in contrast to Macbeth's hollow expressions of grief. The image of a “great hand” suggests a powerful, protective God, and the verb “stand” implies firmness and moral solidity.
quotes.c: The divine right of kings meant that treason was a sin as well as a crime, so his vow aligns him with order.
quotes.q: In the great hand of God I stand
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 3, after the murder is discovered

quotes.a: The suspicion shows Banquo understands what Macbeth has done, but the line is delivered in private. The adverb “foully” echoes the “foul” and “fair” theme of the play, and his silence leaves questions about complicity or caution.
quotes.c: Speaking against a king without proof was dangerous in a Jacobean court, which supports a cautious reading.

quotes.a: The tree metaphor links Banquo to growth and family continuity, which contrasts with the barren images used for Macbeth. The phrase shows that he allows himself hope, and that the prophecy is the main reason that Macbeth fears him.
quotes.c: Flattery of James I, who was believed to descend from Banquo.
quotes.q: root and father / Of many kings

quotes.a: The repeated imperative “fly” creates a breathless, urgent rhythm, and the adjective “good” shows tenderness. His final act is to protect his son, so he dies as a father and a patriot, and his sacrifice ensures the survival of his line.
quotes.c: Family and succession mattered deeply to Jacobean politics; saving the heir saves the future.
quotes.q: Fly, good Fleance, fly, fly, fly!

quotes.a: Macbeth's phrase makes the ghost grotesquely physical, with matted hair as evidence of murder. The adjective “gory” is a graphic and almost childlike term which suggests horror out of control. It also shows that his guilt is expressed through the body.
quotes.c: Ghosts of murdered men demanded vengeance in revenge tragedy, a popular Jacobean genre.
quotes.ref: Act 3 Sc 4, Macbeth to the ghost

quotes.a: The compound adjective suggests hair clotted with blood, and Banquo's smile as he points to the line of kings shows that his murder has not ended his line. The image is a final proof that Macbeth is powerless against the future.
quotes.c: The vision of a royal line moving toward the present would flatter the king in the audience.
quotes.ref: Act 4 Sc 1, the show of kings

summary: Understand Banquo as Macbeth's foil: noble, sceptical and loyal where Macbeth is ambitious and compromised, and as the ancestor of the Stuart kings whose murder and return as a ghost carry the play's ideas of guilt, kingship and the future.

terms.d: A character who contrasts with another in order to highlight particular qualities.
When the audience knows something the characters do not, as with the “temple-haunting martlet” speech at Duncan's doomed castle.
A prediction about the future; in this play ambiguous and open to interpretation.
Using ambiguous language to mislead while claiming to speak the truth; the witches' prophecies behave this way.
A line of rulers from the same family; the line of Banquo's descendants threatens Macbeth's hold on the throne.
Involvement in a wrongdoing by silence or support; a possible reading of Banquo's silence in 3.1.
A figure of speech which says one thing is another; Banquo uses “seeds of time”.
Words spoken by a character that the audience hears but others on stage do not.
A spirit of the dead; in 3.4 it can be read as supernatural or as a projection of guilt.
